analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon emissions at $30 per ton and sends most of the money back to low-income households and corporations via tax cuts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 3 cosponsors, referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee of $30 per metric ton on carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels and large facilities, rising 4% above inflation each year. Most of the revenue would go to monthly energy refunds for low- and middle-income households, plus a program to help coal workers who lose their jobs. It would also gradually cut the corporate income tax rate from 35% down to 28%, and add fees on imports and refunds for exports so U.S. companies are not disadvantaged against foreign competitors.
analysis.who_benefits: Households earning up to 200% of the poverty line — especially those on SNAP, SSI, or Medicare drug subsidies — would receive monthly cash energy refunds to cover the higher energy prices the carbon tax creates. Coal workers facing layoffs would get retraining, relocation, early retirement, and health benefits for 10 years. All corporations would benefit from a lower income tax rate. Everyone would benefit from reduced greenhouse gas emissions.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $30 per metric ton excise tax on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel products and large emitting facilities, rising each year at 4% above inflation, to discourage pollution [S2][S3].

Creates a Low-Income Energy Cost Mitigation Program providing monthly cash energy refunds to households at or below 200% of the poverty line, largely those enrolled in SNAP, SSI, or Medicare low-income subsidy programs, with refunds extending further into middle incomes if revenues exceed program costs [S2][S3].
Allows up to 2% of revenues for 10 years to fund retraining, relocation, early retirement, and health benefits for coal workers displaced by the tax [S2][S3].
Gradually lowers the corporate income tax rate from 32% in 2016 to 28% after 2019, reducing the tax burden on corporations as the carbon tax raises revenue [S2][S3].

Includes border adjustments — refunds for exporters and fees on imports equal to what the tax would have cost — to protect U.S. manufacturers from competing against goods produced without a carbon price [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters pay the tax directly, and those costs would be passed to consumers in the form of higher prices for gasoline, electricity, and heating. Households above the refund eligibility thresholds would bear the higher energy costs without compensation, though the bill extends refunds into middle incomes when revenue is surplus. Corporations receiving the rate cut are effectively paid for in part by the carbon tax revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and higher-income energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The carbon tax would raise energy prices for every household and business; households above the income thresholds for the refund program would absorb those costs without compensation [S2][S3].

Coal and other fossil fuel industries would face sharply higher costs, with concentrated job losses in coal-dependent regions; the bill offsets this for workers with only up to 2% of revenues over 10 years [S2][S3].
The bill pairs the tax with a corporate income tax cut to 28%, meaning a significant share of the carbon tax revenue would go to corporations rather than to households [S2][S3].

A new monthly refund program administered through state agencies would add substantial administrative complexity, though the federal government would reimburse states for full administrative costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine attempt at a revenue-neutral-style carbon tax that shields low-income households from energy cost increases and compensates displaced coal workers, while also cutting corporate taxes. The design is more protective of ordinary people than most carbon tax proposals, since refunds are automatic and extend into middle incomes when revenue allows. The main trade-off is that middle- and higher-income households pay more for energy without compensation, and the corporate tax cut directs part of the revenue away from household relief. As with any carbon tax, the environmental benefit depends on how much emissions actually fall.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. John Delaney introduced the bill on May 1, 2015, joined by Reps. Huffman, Cartwright, and Polis as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and in addition to the Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters never faced the $30-per-ton tax, and corporations never faced the offsetting restructuring of the tax code. Low-income households and coal communities got none of the refunds or assistance the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-led committees to which it was referred took no action, and there is no record of any Republican support.

industries.industry: Coal producers and coal-fired power plants
industries.note: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel, so the $30-per-ton tax would hit it hardest and accelerate plant closures. The bill's worker-assistance fund acknowledges this, but the industry's interest in avoiding the tax runs against the public's interest in cutting emissions. [S2][S3]
Their products would carry the tax at the supply-chain chokepoints, raising prices for their customers. Industry avoided the tax entirely when the bill died. [S2][S3]

The bill cuts the corporate income tax rate to 28%, financed in part by carbon tax revenue. Energy-intensive manufacturers gain from border adjustments that shield them from foreign competitors without a carbon price. [S2][S3]
Coal workers would lose jobs as the tax shrinks coal demand, but the bill funds retraining, relocation, early retirement, and health benefits for 10 years from up to 2% of revenues. [S2][S3]
